body_en:
*Season Stats 2025, part 1 of 4. The series by Chris Pracher: **Part 1: Understanding advanced stats** · Part 2: Season Stats 2025, offense deep dive · Part 3: Defense deep dive · Part 4: All advanced stats at a glance.*

## Understanding advanced stats: a short glossary of metrics for Niners fans

Anyone who takes football seriously today can no longer ignore so-called advanced stats, because yards and touchdowns have long ceased to be enough to explain why a team wins or loses. But what actually lies behind abbreviations like EPA, DVOA or CPOE that show up in every other analysis? This glossary explains the most important metrics concisely and in four dimensions, namely name, source, derivation and meaning, so that you can read our season reviews with the necessary tools.

To start with a thought: Kyle Shanahan calls a run. Christian McCaffrey takes the ball and is brought down after 4 yards. In principle, 4 yards is fine, since 3 x 4 yards makes 12 yards and therefore a first down. If it always goes like that, perfect. But it is not always that simple, because it depends on the circumstances. 4 yards on 3rd and 3 is good, or at least enough. On 4th and 5 or 3rd and 10, though, that is clearly too little given the situation. Another example: an 8-yard pass sounds pretty good at first, considering that only a few QBs average more than 8 yards per throw. But an 8-yard pass no longer looks so good if it comes on 4th and 12 in the final two minutes of a one-possession game. Both examples show that the raw numbers often tell only half the truth. Advanced stats were developed to get closer to that truth.

## The foundations: team metrics

**EPA / expected points added** (RBSDM/Sumersports, originally Brian Burke). The derivation sounds more complicated than it is: every game situation has an expected point value based on down, distance, field position and time, and EPA simply measures how much a single play changes that expected value. A positive value is good for the offense, a negative one good for the defense. The idea behind it is strikingly simple: EPA measures the actual net value of a play instead of just counting yards gained.

**EPA/play** (RBSDM/Sumersports). Dividing total EPA by the number of plays gives you the gold standard of efficiency measurement. The value filters out the statistical noise of pure volume numbers like total yards and is considered by many analysts the single most meaningful number of all.

**Success rate** (RBSDM/Sumersports). It measures not magnitude but reliability: the percentage of plays with positive EPA. While EPA/play can be skewed by individual big plays, success rate shows how consistently a team stays "on schedule," i.e. how often a play actually puts it in a better position.

**DVOA / defense-adjusted value over average** (FTN Football Almanac, originally Aaron Schatz at Football Outsiders). Its derivation is the most elaborate in this group: DVOA compares every single play with the historical league average in exactly the same situation and fully adjusts for the strength of the opponent. The result states as a percentage how much better or worse than average a unit was. The sign logic matters: for offense and special teams, positive is good; for defense, negative is good.

## The quarterback: efficiency and risk

**CPOE / completion percentage over expected** (RBSDM). For every pass, an expected completion rate can be calculated from distance, receiver separation and defender proximity; CPOE is the difference between the actual and the expected rate. A positive value means a quarterback completes passes that statistically should have been incomplete, a pure measure of accuracy and anticipation.

**Pressure-to-sack rate** (PFF/SIS). It measures the percentage of situations in which opposing pressure actually turns into a sack. The insight behind it may surprise many: sacks are to a large extent a quarterback stat, not just a matter of the offensive line. A low rate shows excellent pocket presence, a high one that a quarterback practically invites sacks.

**ESPN QBR** (ESPN Analytics). Unlike the outdated passer rating, QBR includes all of a quarterback's actions, passes, runs, scrambles and turnovers, adjusts for opponent strength and filters out garbage time. On its 0 to 100 scale, 50 marks the league average, and anything above 70 is considered elite.

**PFF pass grade** (PFF). Analysts grade every single play on a scale from -2 to +2 and normalize the result to 0 to 100. The key point: performance is graded independently of the outcome, so a perfect pass that gets dropped still counts positively.

**Big-time throw rate / BTT%** (PFF, also listed in the FTN almanac). It captures the percentage of passes with excellent placement and excellent timing, usually deep downfield or into extremely tight windows. It speaks to big-play potential: the value shows how often a quarterback is capable of the elite throws that can decide a game on their own.

**Turnover-worthy play rate / TWP%** (PFF/FTN). The counterpart to BTT%, since it measures not the artistry but the risk: the percentage of plays that should have been an interception even if the defender dropped it, plus fumbles clearly caused by the quarterback. Its message is especially valuable as an early warning system, because a quarterback with few interceptions but a high TWP% has simply been lucky with opposing defenders so far and is unlikely to sustain those turnover numbers.

## Running backs and receivers: individual impact

**RYOE / rushing yards over expected** (Next Gen Stats). Using tracking data of all blockers and defenders, an expected number of yards can be calculated at the moment of the handoff; RYOE is the difference from reality. The value thus shows how many yards a running back generates purely through his own vision and physicality, regardless of how well the offensive line blocked.

**YPRR / yards per route run** (PFF). Total receiving yards divided by the number of routes run. Because the value strips out pure volume, it is considered perhaps the most important receiver metric of all: anything above 2.0 is very good, above 2.5 is elite.

**Target share** (Sumersports). The share of team targets that goes to a particular receiver. It measures his importance in the passing game and at the same time serves as context for efficiency values like YPRR; a high value combined with high efficiency is the hallmark of a true No. 1 receiver.

**ESPN receiver tracking metrics** (ESPN). A composite score from 0 to 99 that combines the three phases of receiver play: getting open (open score), catching (catch score) and yards after the catch (YAC score). A value of 99 represents absolute elite performance.

## The offensive line: the most thankless stat

**PFF pass block grade and run block grade** (PFF). An offensive lineman's performance was long hard to capture in numbers, which is why PFF relies on an error-based grading system here: analysts grade every single snap on a scale from 0 to 100, with no bonus for a block that is simply held but clear deductions for a lost one, and an allowed sack weighs the most. The message is more robust than pure sack numbers because hurries and hits are included as well: above 70 is considered good, above 80 elite, both in pass and run blocking.

**Pass block win rate and run block win rate** (ESPN/Next Gen Stats). These two tracking metrics measure blocking against a simple success threshold: in pass protection, a block counts as won if it holds for at least 2.5 seconds, the critical mark within which a quarterback should get rid of the ball on average; in the run game, if the blocker successfully drives his opponent out of the hole. Their advantage is that they are easy to grasp, since they can be shown both individually and for the unit as a whole.

**TruePassSets blocking efficiency** (PFF). Perhaps the most reliable of all OL metrics, because it consistently filters out situationally "easy" blocks: only true dropback situations are graded, while play-action plays, screens and rollouts are excluded, since they artificially distort lineman performance. That is exactly why past TruePassSets values are a particularly strong predictor of future performance.

**PFSN OL impact** (Pro Football Network). The attempt to pour everything into a single grade with a letter: the value combines pass and run blocking metrics at a ratio of 60 to 40 and takes into account pressures, true dropback situations and time to pressure. Its value lies in fair comparison, because it places linemen independently of scheme or team performance and also ranks them within their position groups (tackle, guard, center).

## Front and secondary: the work without the ball

**Pass rush win rate** (PFF/ESPN). The percentage of pass rushes in which a defender beats his blocker within 2.5 seconds. Because the threshold applies regardless of whether the quarterback gets rid of the ball quickly, it is considered the best measure of a pass rusher's pure quality.

**Run stop rate** (PFF). The percentage of run snaps on which a defender records a "stop," i.e. a tackle that constitutes a failure for the offense. This value is crucial especially for defensive tackles and edge rushers on first down.

**Coverage snaps per target** (PFF/SIS). It indicates how many snaps a defender spends in coverage before he is thrown at even once. A high value is a badge of honor: it shows that quarterbacks deliberately avoid a corner of the field, as you see with true shutdown cornerbacks.

**Rec% / reception rate** (PFF). The percentage of targets against a defender that result in a catch. Here, less is more: an elite cornerback is below 50 to 55 percent, though the value should always be read in the context of the quality of the opposing receivers.

Anyone who has internalized these roughly one and a half dozen terms will read every modern football analysis with different eyes, and will also understand why our season reviews of the offense and defense sometimes reach verdicts that would never follow from the box score alone. Because that is exactly the point of advanced stats: they separate what a team really does well from what merely looks like a nice number.

## Quick reference of the key abbreviations

| Abbreviation | Measures | Source |
|---|---|---|
| EPA/play | Efficiency per play | RBSDM |
| Success rate | Consistency, staying on schedule | RBSDM |
| DVOA | Efficiency vs. league, opponent-adjusted | FTN Almanac |
| CPOE | Passing accuracy over expected | RBSDM |
| Pressure-to-sack rate | How the QB handles pressure | PFF/SIS |
| ESPN QBR | Overall QB value, context-adjusted | ESPN |
| Big-time throw rate | Share of elite throws | PFF/FTN |
| Turnover-worthy play rate | Risky throws (deserved INTs) | PFF/FTN |
| RYOE | Rushing yards over expected | Next Gen Stats |
| YPRR | Yards per route run | PFF |
| Target share | Share of team targets | Sumersports |
| PFF block grade | Blocking quality per snap | PFF |
| Pass rush win rate | Quality of the pass rusher | PFF/ESPN |
| Coverage snaps/target | Respect in coverage | PFF/SIS |
| Rec% | Allowed catch rate | PFF |

Go Niners!
